newsitem.title: EGYPT: Israeli, Arab business people meet at conference.
newsitem.headline: Israeli, Arab business people meet at conference.

text.p: The Egyptian banker stepped up almost furtively to the Israeli banking display on Wednesday, quickly picking up some literature and preparing to walk on.
"Please take a sweet," said Bank Hapoalim's Joel Rabinowitz, pointing to a basket of Israeli candy on his stand. The Egyptian paused, smiled and took the toffee.

"I thought I'd just be sitting here but people are taking the material," Rabinowitz said, a day after Palestinians raised the prospect of a "spontaneous" boycott of Israel by Arab business executives at a Middle East economic conference.
Candy might be an ice-breaker but it is no deal-maker and Israeli businessmen said they did not expect to sign many contracts at the three-day meeting ending on Thursday.

"There are a lot of individual meetings," said Yoram Blizovsky of the Manufacturers' Association of Israel at the busy Israeli business centre in the conference lobby. "This isn't a place to sign deals. It's a place to meet people."
He said a group of Israeli business people had met representatives of 14 Egyptian trade organisations in a hotel on Tuesday.
"We discussed relations and how to deepen economic ties," Blizovsky said. "I can't say the political situation was healthy. There were those who tried to link the political situation with business."
As the second day of the conference started, the Israeli centre, run by Israel's Export Institute, was no less busy than the Palestinian one.
Arab business people, however, appeared to prefer to walk along the Israeli perimeter, examining booklets of economic statistics and projects, rather than step inside.

But one Israeli attendant said Egyptian, Jordanian and Qatari business executives had visited the centre. Egypt and Jordan have peace treaties with Israel but Qatar has said it would not open a planned trade office in Tel Aviv until progress was made on peace.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whose right-wing policies rejecting the concept of land-for-peace have angered Arabs, and the United States have lobbied wary Israeli business people to attend the Cairo conference.
Calls by left-wing Egyptian professional and political groups calling for Israelis to be shunned made headlines in Israel.

"We came to this conference with some trepidation...because we were getting mixed messages from the Egyptian government and the private sector," said Dan Gillerman, chairman of the Federation of the Israeli Chamber of Commerce.
Hotel problems also plagued the Israelis, sensitive to any perceived snub.
Blizovsky said a Cairo hotel lost reservations for 45 leading members of the Israeli delegation.

"Two days before the conference we tried to check if the bookings were in order. They said: 'No Israelis'...saying we didn't send cash. Have you ever heard of having to guarantee a reservation with cash?" he said angrily.
The Egyptian Tourism Ministry was called in to intervene and rooms were found elsewhere.
